content: This typically occurs when bright sunlight is reflected off snow or ice. The risk of snow blindness is particularly high in polar regions and at elevated altitudes, as UV intensity increases by approximately 5% with every 1,000 feet of elevation gain. This condition is similar to arc eye, which is sometimes experienced by welders. Snow blindness can be thought of as a sunburn affecting the cornea and conjunctiva. They can range from redness and excessive tearing of the eyes to significant pain, a gritty sensation, and swelling that may cause the eyes to shut. In severe cases, snow blindness can result in permanent vision loss. Historically, the Inuit developed protective goggles made from caribou antler to prevent snow blindness. These goggles were designed to fit the contours of the face and featured a large groove to accommodate the nose. A narrow slit was cut into the goggles to allow only a small amount of light to enter. The goggles were secured to the head using a cord made from caribou sinew. To prevent snow blindness during activities such as trekking, mountaineering, or skiing, it is recommended to wear sunglasses with the following features: Lenses that provide 99-100% UV absorption. Lenses made of polycarbonate or CR-39 material. Visible light transmittance limited to 5-10%. Large lenses that fit closely to the face and fully cover the eyes. Sunglasses should be worn even on overcast days, as UV rays can penetrate through clouds. In emergencies, if sunglasses are lost or damaged, makeshift goggles can be created by cutting slits into dark fabric or tape folded back onto itself. The following steps are recommended: Avoid rubbing the eyes and remove any contact lenses. Take an oral pain reliever, such as ibuprofen, to manage discomfort. Protect the eyes by covering them with soft, thick cloth pads or gauze bandages to minimize irritation from eyelid movement and shield them from light. Resting in a dark room is ideal. Apply cold, wet compresses to the eyes to relieve burning sensations. Monitor the injury at intervals of approximately 12 hours. Remove the protective dressing once the eyes can remain open comfortably. Continue wearing sunglasses outdoors until all symptoms have resolved completely.
